pages.text:
*Jun's phone says: charging. Nari's river says: brown, but going down.*

The sound came before the truck. A low rumble, then a bounce, a thud, a bounce. The gravel road shook. Uncle’s blue truck rounded the bend at speed, its tires spraying mud that hit the concrete pier. He did not slow down. He stopped, the engine still growling, and jumped out before the truck had finished rocking.

He was broad and wet. He smelled of rain, wet earth, and the river. He opened his arms.

Nari went first. She collided with his chest, and he lifted her off the ground, one arm around her waist, the other bracing her back. He held her there, tight, his face buried in her messy hair.

Then Jun. He stepped forward, stiff at first, unsure. Uncle’s arms wrapped around him, lifting him too. Jun’s muddy sneakers dangled in the air. He could feel the rapid thud of Uncle’s heart against his ribs. It was faster than his own.

Uncle said nothing. He just held them, both of them, shaking slightly. The rain dripped from his straw hat onto Jun’s glasses. Jun looked up. His father’s brother was crying.
pages.image: Uncle, a broad man in a navy work shirt and straw hat, hugs Nari and Jun together in his arms on a muddy road beside his blue truck; Nari and Jun both wear orange life vests, Nari with her long braid and yellow shirt, Jun in glasses and a white T-shirt; Uncle wears no life vest.

pages.text:
They climbed into the back of the truck. The Pear sat on top, secured under a heavy canvas tarp that had flapped in the wind. Nari tied her braid tighter. Jun pulled his knees up to his chest.

The truck bounced over the ruts. Rain drifted sideways, blurring the world into grey streaks. They passed the rice paddies, where the water was high and brown. They passed the levee.

It stood.

It was a wall of sandbags, stacked high, reinforced with wood and wire. Dozens of neighbors stood along it, holding the line, their boots squelching in the mud. As the truck passed, several waved. One man lifted a thumb.

They drove past the village hall. Every light was on. Through the windows, Jun saw the shapes of adults, moving, talking, checking phones. The door was open. Voices drifted out, sharp and worried.

Then the road turned, and the house appeared.

The porch light was on. It cut a warm, yellow cone into the grey morning. The door was closed. But the gate at the front of the yard was swinging open, banging softly against the post.

Jun’s phone, dead and useless, sat in its pouch. He did not reach for it. He watched the gate.
pages.image: The interior of a moving blue truck bed, with Nari and Jun huddled under a tarp covering the wooden boat, looking out a side window at a muddy levee reinforced with sandbags and waving neighbors in the rain.

pages.text:
Halmoni was already at the gate before the truck engine even coughed to a stop. Her purple sun visor sat crooked on her head, and her grey perm was wild, damp, and sticking out in every direction from the rain. Mud splattered her floral blouse, and she did not wait for the tires to crunch into the gravel.

She ran.

Her rubber slippers slapped loudly against the wet ground, and she moved faster than Jun had ever seen her move, her knees bending and her arms stretching out wide. She hit them like a sudden, heavy wave breaking against a low wall.

Jun and Nari were folded completely into her. Her face pressed against Nari’s shoulder, then against Jun’s cheek, and her whole body was shaking.

"Aigoo!" she said, and the word came out as a sob. "Aigoo, aigoo!"

She pulled back, her hands gripping their shoulders tightly. Her eyes were wet, and she looked at them, really looked at them, until the scolding rushed out mixed with tears.

"Foolish children," she said. "So foolish. Do you know what I did? I stopped cooking. I stopped breathing. I was counting your steps!"

She slapped their backs, though it was not really a slap at all, but a hug delivered with the full force of a grandmother who had just lost everything and found it again. Nari looked at Jun, her eyes wide, because she had never seen her grandmother cry before.
pages.image: Halmoni, a small elderly woman in a mud-stained floral blouse and purple visor, hugs Jun and Nari tightly at a wooden garden gate in the rain, her face buried in Nari's shoulder, her hands gripping their arms.

pages.text:
Harabeoji stood on the porch, his striped shirt dark with rain and his thin white moustache damp. He did not run, nor did he shout, but simply watched the truck stop and Uncle unload the cousins.

His eyes moved to the boat.

He walked down the steps, his tall black rubber boots making a heavy, rhythmic sound on the wood. Stopping in front of the Pear, he saw the tarp tied tight and the rope knotted securely. It was the knot they had made together.

His finger traced the loop of the rope. Then he looked at the two orange life vests hanging from the gunwale, and finally at the plank they had used as a paddle.

The rain dripped from his cap as he waited, his face unreadable.

"Vests on?" he asked, his voice low.

"Yes," said Nari.

"Stayed with the boat?"

"Yes," said Jun.

Harabeoji nodded once, a single, sharp motion. He did not hug them, nor did he scold them. Turning, he walked inside, the screen door sliding shut behind him with a sigh.
pages.image: Harabeoji, a thin elderly man in a striped shirt and black rubber boots, stands on the muddy ground beside a wooden boat under a tarp, touching the rope knot with his finger, while Jun and Nari watch him from the truck bed.

pages.text:
Halmoni made food.

It was bibimbap, bowls of rice piled high with warm vegetables and a fried egg on top, finished with a generous spoonful of red pepper paste. The smell filled the small dining room, warm and spicy and safe.

Jun sat on the mat in the warmest corner of the room. The ondol floor was cool under his shorts, but the air was thick with steam. He ate until his stomach was full and his hands were still shaking.

Halmoni sat across from him. She watched him eat. Then she picked up his bowl.

"Grounded," she said.

Jun froze.

"No screens," she said. "No questions. Three days."

She put the bowl down. Her face softened.

"And I love you," she added.

Nari, from the next mat, looked up. She had a piece of scallion hanging from her mouth.

"You're not grounded," she said. "You're loved."

Jun looked at Halmoni. He looked at Nari. He pushed his glasses up his nose.

"Both," he said.

Halmoni smiled. It was a small, tired smile. But it was real.
pages.image: Jun, a thin boy in round glasses and a white T-shirt, sits on a floor mat eating from a bowl of food, while Halmoni, in her floral blouse, sits across from him smiling, and Nari, in her yellow T-shirt, watches from the next mat with a piece of food in her mouth.
